planting.note: Start seed in a cold frame or indoors in late winter and transplant young onion sets out while soil is still cool, giving this long-day type a full spring to bulb before heat sets in.

directions: This flattened, golden-skinned sweet onion from the Figueres district of Girona in Catalonia is prized for mild, low-pungency flesh that is traditionally eaten raw, thinly sliced, with just bread and olive oil. Grow it in loose, fertile ground with steady moisture through bulb swell, then cut back watering once the tops begin to yellow and fall over to concentrate sugars and cure the skins. Harvest when roughly half the foliage has flopped, then field-cure for several days before braiding or storing in a dry, airy spot, since the thin skins and high sugar content make this variety a poor long-term keeper compared with pungent storage onions.
sources: Institut Català de la Vinya i el Vi / Generalitat de Catalunya agricultural registers
Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Catalan onion varieties

common_name: Fuentes de Ebro Onion (Cebolla Dulce de Fuentes de Ebro)

planting.note: Sow in protected beds in winter and transplant in early spring; this PGI-protected onion needs the Ebro valley's long, steadily warming season to reach its full globe size.

directions: Grown under European PGI protection around Fuentes de Ebro in Aragón, this large, pale-skinned onion is famous for an exceptionally sweet, almost fruity flesh with very low pungency, making it the base of the region's cold ensalada de cebolla. It needs deep, well-worked alluvial-type soil and consistent irrigation through bulb development, since the thin cell walls that give it sweetness also make it prone to stress cracking in uneven moisture. Harvest as soon as tops fall and skins set, then use promptly or refrigerate, as the same delicate structure that makes it sweet also makes it one of the shortest-storing onions grown commercially.
sources: European Commission PDO/PGI Register
Diputación General de Aragón agricultural extension

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and stake heavily once transplanted, since the deeply lobed, flattened fruit of this Catalan heirloom grows large and heavy on indeterminate vines.

directions: Named for the serrated mountain outside Barcelona, this heirloom produces deeply ribbed, flattened pink-red beefsteak fruit with a thin skin and a pronounced acidic-sweet balance that Catalan cooks favor for pa amb tomàquet and fresh salads. Provide a sturdy trellis or cage, since vigorous indeterminate vines and heavy fruit clusters need support to keep fruit off the ground. Keep watering even through fruit set to avoid blossom-end rot and catfacing in the deep lobes, and pick at full color while still slightly firm for the best texture in raw preparations.
sources: Institut de Recerca i Tecnologia Agroalimentàries (IRTA) tomato germplasm collections
Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Catalan tomato varieties

common_name: Penjar Tomato (Tomàquet de Penjar / Tomate de Colgar)

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant after frost into lean, dry-farmed conditions; vines are grown through summer specifically to be harvested green-mature in autumn for winter storage rather than fresh summer eating.

directions: This small, thick-skinned Catalan and Valencian landrace tomato is bred specifically for storage, not fresh slicing: fruit is picked while still firm and barely turning color, then braided by the stem into ristras and hung indoors, where it slowly ripens and keeps for months into winter. Grow it lean, with minimal irrigation once established, since dry-farmed conditions concentrate the thick skin and low water content that make it such a reliable keeper. Harvest the whole vine or individual clusters just as color begins to break, and store the hanging fruit in a cool, airy, dark space, checking occasionally and removing any that spoil.
sources: Institut de Recerca i Tecnologia Agroalimentàries (IRTA) tomato germplasm collections
Generalitat de Catalunya Departament d'Agricultura landrace registers

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; this Alicante market tomato is traditionally grown under light greenhouse cover for an extended, humidity-buffered fruiting season.

directions: Named for the town of Mutxamel near Alicante, this smooth-shouldered, pale green-to-pink beefsteak tomato is a staple of Valencian market gardens, grown for a balanced, low-acid flesh with few seeds that holds up well in thick slices. Stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines and keep moisture consistent through fruit development, since irregular watering tends to show up as cracking around the shoulders on this smooth-skinned type. Harvest when fruit has colored but is still firm, and expect strong production into early autumn where summers run long and hot.
sources: Institut Valencià d'Investigacions Agràries (IVIA)
Generalitat Valenciana Conselleria d'Agricultura landrace documentation

planting.note: Establish from rooted offshoots or crowns in autumn along the irrigated Ebro riverbanks of Navarra, where mild winters let plants push the small, tender buds prized for canning.

directions: Grown along the fertile Ebro floodplain around Tudela in Navarra, this artichoke is harvested young and small, often as whole baby buds or hearts, and is the classic ingredient behind Spain's prized jarred corazones de alcachofa. Give it deep, rich, constantly moist soil, since the region's river-fed irrigation is what produces the characteristically tender, nearly spineless bud that needs little trimming. Harvest buds while still tight and only a few inches across for the best canning quality, cutting continuously through the cool growing season to encourage further lateral budding.
sources: European Commission PDO/PGI Register
Gobierno de Navarra agricultural extension

planting.note: Plant rooted offshoots in autumn in the sandy coastal soils around Benicarló in Castellón, where mild Mediterranean winters allow buds to mature from late autumn through spring.

directions: This PGI-protected artichoke from the Castellón coast produces compact, tightly closed, nearly thornless heads prized fresh across Valencia for dishes like alcachofas a la plancha. Coastal sandy-loam soils with good drainage but regular irrigation suit it best, and plants benefit from a dry summer dormancy followed by a strong autumn watering to trigger the main bud flush. Harvest the primary terminal bud first, then continue cutting smaller lateral buds as they form through winter and into spring, discarding any that have begun to open and toughen.
sources: European Commission PDO/PGI Register
Generalitat Valenciana Conselleria d'Agricultura landrace documentation

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since fruit needs a long warm season to fully ripen red before the traditional wood-smoke drying that gives this León variety its character.

directions: Grown in the Bierzo district of León, this mild, thick-walled red pepper is the raw material for pimentón de Bierzo, a smoked paprika cured over oak and chestnut wood fires rather than sun-dried as in Murcia. Let fruit ripen fully to deep red on the plant before harvest, since underripe pods lack the sugar needed to develop the variety's characteristic sweet, smoky depth once dried and ground. After picking, fruit is traditionally slow-smoked over several days, then ground to a fine powder; home growers without smoking facilities can still dry pods whole for a milder, sweet paprika substitute.
sources: European Commission PDO/PGI Register — Pimentón de Bierzo
Consejo Regulador de la Denominación de Origen Protegida Pimentón de Bierzo

planting.note: Direct-sow in early spring on the dry plains around Fuentesaúco in Zamora as soon as the ground can be worked, relying on winter soil moisture to carry the crop through its mostly unirrigated growing season.

directions: This large, thin-skinned, pale chickpea from the Zamora plateau is prized for cooking down to a notably creamy, buttery texture without needing the long pre-soak many chickpeas require. It thrives in the region's deep clay-loam soils under dry-farmed conditions, tolerating drought well once established, though a wet spring during flowering can both help yields and risk fungal disease, so good air movement between rows matters. Harvest whole plants once pods have dried and rattle, then thresh, and favor minimal irrigation throughout to avoid diluting the dense, starchy texture this variety is known for.
sources: European Commission PDO/PGI Register — Garbanzo de Fuentesaúco
Junta de Castilla y León agricultural extension

planting.note: Sow bulb-type seedlings in spring, then let them bulb fully through summer before cutting back; the same plants resprout new white shanks that are repeatedly mounded with soil through autumn and winter.

directions: Calçots are grown in a distinctive two-stage method unique to the Valls area of Tarragona: a regular sweet onion bulb is grown to maturity, cut back hard, and then regrown from the same root, with soil mounded progressively up the regrowing shoots to blanch them into long, thick, sweet white shanks. Keep soil consistently moist through both the bulbing and regrowth stages, since dry spells toughen the blanched shanks that are the entire point of the crop. Harvest by pulling the whole plant once shanks reach finger thickness, then traditionally char them whole over an open flame and peel back the blackened outer layer before eating with romesco sauce.
sources: European Commission PDO/PGI Register — Calçot de Valls
Generalitat de Catalunya Departament d'Agricultura
